plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to run a small agent that checks 3 to 5 competitor web pages every day, spots what changed, and sends you a short plain-English summary, with every claim in that summary pointing back to the exact page it came from.
plan.horizon14: Later, around day 14, you could add more sources (news, job listings, app store notes) and a weekly roll-up instead of daily noise.
plan.horizon28: Later still, around day 28, you could let the agent sort changes by what matters to you (pricing, new features, hires) and ignore the rest.

picture.name: a newspaper clipping service
picture.line: Think of the agent as a person you pay to read the same 5 newspapers every morning, cut out only the stories about your rivals, and leave a short note on your desk.

chapters.title: What an agent is, and what it is not
chapters.covers: An agent is a program that runs on its own, on a schedule, and calls an AI model to read and write text. You see the 4 parts: a trigger (the alarm clock), sources (the newspapers), the model (the reader), and the output (the note on your desk).
chapters.outcome: You can draw the 4 boxes of a competitor-tracking agent on paper and say what each one does.

chapters.title: Choosing who to watch and where to look
chapters.covers: Pick 3 to 5 competitors and, for each, 1 or 2 pages that actually change: pricing, changelog, blog, careers. You learn why fewer, better pages beat a list of 50.
chapters.outcome: You can write a list of 3 to 5 competitors with 1 or 2 exact web addresses each, and say why each page is worth reading.

chapters.title: Fetching a page and keeping a copy
chapters.covers: The agent downloads each page as text and saves it with the date. This is the clipping: without a saved copy you cannot tell what changed tomorrow.
chapters.outcome: You can fetch one competitor page, save its text to a file named with today's date, and open it to check it worked.

chapters.title: Spotting what changed
chapters.covers: Compare today's copy with yesterday's and keep only the lines that are new or gone. A diff (a line-by-line comparison) is the clipping service's scissors.
chapters.outcome: You can run a comparison between 2 saved copies of a page and list exactly which lines were added or removed.

chapters.title: Asking the model to explain the change
chapters.covers: Send only the changed lines to an AI model with a short, strict instruction: say what changed, in 2 sentences, and quote the source line. You learn why giving the model less text gives you better answers.
chapters.outcome: You can write a prompt (the instruction you give the model) that turns a diff into a 2-sentence plain-English summary with a quoted source.

chapters.title: Running it every day without you
chapters.covers: Put the fetch, compare and summarise steps on a daily schedule, and deliver the result somewhere you will actually see it: an email, a chat message, or a file. The alarm clock goes on.
chapters.outcome: You can set the agent to run once a day on its own and receive the summary without opening a terminal.

chapters.title: Catching the agent when it is wrong
chapters.covers: Pages break, sites block you, models make things up. You add 3 checks: did the fetch work, is the diff empty, and does every claim in the summary quote a real line. Trust comes from checks, not from hope.
chapters.outcome: You can read one day's summary, trace each claim back to its source line, and spot a fetch failure or an invented claim within 2 minutes.
